comments.text:
See the thing about the 3080 Ti is this: yes I get it, it's very expensive and you can call me a fool for buying the TUF Gaming OC version of it. However, it really shouldn't be compared to a regular 3080. It is about 10% faster than a 3080 on average for 70% more money. That is a stupidly, hilariously horrible deal, yes. However, it starts to make more sense when you compare it to the 3090. At best, it's 2% slower than the 3090, yet it is 20% cheaper and has half the VRAM. The 3090 is good for gaming, but it's designed for so much more. 

If all you do is gaming, and you want the best gaming performance and can afford it, by all means you should sacrifice that UNNOTICABLE 2% performance from the 3090 and step down to a 3080 Ti. However, if you also do creative stuff like video editing, encoding, blender, 3D Modelling etc. then the 3090 is the card for you. Do not get a 3090 if all you do is gaming as it is a total waste of money and it's 20% more expensive than the 3080 Ti which, again, is only 2% slower. 

So do you really want to pay 20% more for 2% gain? I didn't think so. The 3090 does much, much better in these 3D modelling, video editing etc applications than the 3080 Ti. So, instead of comparing the 3080 Ti to the 3080, compare it to the 3090 and it makes a bit more sense. Of course, most people will buy the vastly more affordable 3070, as even the 3080 is pretty crazy expensive compared to the 3070. I do not support Nvidia with its price gouging, by the way, I'm just giving my 2 cents, and it can't be said that I'm totally wrong. 


TL;DR: RTX 3080, 3080 Ti and 3090 are all stupidly expensive. The 3080 has the power to SOMEWHAT justify its price, while the 3090 is excellent for those who do more than just gaming. So instead of comparing the 3080 Ti to the 3080, compare it to the 3090 which is 2% better and 20% more expensive. For the best gaming results IF YOU CAN AFFORD, get a 3080 Ti instead of a 3090 if all you do is gaming, as you're spending 20% LESS for basically the same performance. Again, I do not support what Nvidia is doing to us, this is pretty much robbery.

comments.text:
Huge fan of this channel but I think the script for this video is a bit emotional/silly at times.  Let the data speak for it self - the primary value proposition of this channel is trustworthy, comprehensive data (which I truly appreciate and rely on), and clear explanations/summaries of new technologies, etc. 

"makes absolutely no sense" - that's an unqualified statement that my guess is kind of annoying to a decent chunk of this audience.  I fully understand the 3080 ti and 3090 are poor value propositions (thanks largely to your data), but saying it "makes absolutely no sense" - I just don't see the point of speaking like that.  For some people, 10% more performance is worth $400.  For many, it's not.  Where else can I get that 10% better performance - are you making a graphics card that is better value?  At the end of the day, I don't lose sight of the fact these companies are making magical products that make life more fun - I have fun with your videos, but not new engineering/product release level of fun... 

The main reason I bring this up is the clarity of the overall video.  For the first 5 minutes of the video, I was under the impression the 3080 Ti was an actual pile of garbage that should be avoided at all costs (yes I probably didn't listen carefully enough but that seemed to be the gist of it).  Then I saw the data and was like ok fine, makes sense - if you're fine paying the money this could be a fun card (especially ROG Strix!).  Also, I would say the semiconductor shortage really isn't Nvidia's fault and frankly many people aren't interested in budget cards right now.  The people want the badass shit right now.  I'm not really mad with this launch or with AMD/Nvidia - I just hope the supply shortages get fixed soon so we can all buy these awesome cards.

comments.text:
I guess this thing's value depends on how you look at it.  If you consider it a slightly cut down 3090 with less vram for $300 less, it's a good relative value in that sense.   My guess is that NVidia figured out that most of the rejected silicon from the 3090 was only very slightly off the mark, and they could fill a niche and sigificantly raise prices.   Now, here's the kicker:  I don't think the price change at MSRP won't affect consumers in the slightest.   What it will do is change who's pockets gets the biggest part of the inflated retail prices.  NVidia will be making more for the same silicon, and the board partners will pass that on to their distributors.  So the distributors and end retailers will make less.  The near $2000 current market retail for a 3080 (or more for a 3090) won't change as a result of this part coming to market.   In fact, you may end up getting the Ti model for the same over inflated prices as the non Ti, just because there isn't any market headroom to charge more.

Of course, if NVidia is coming to market with a metric sh-tton of these cards, they could rock the entire market.  It's in their interest to drive retail prices back down closer to MSRP, as consumers will be "happy" to only get screwed out of a few hundred more dollars instead of $1000 or more on top.

You (We) may not like it because of the high prices, but that is the law of supply and demand.  Once the demand starts dropping the prices will start dropping. 

AMD is going through the same thing.  Only in some ways they have it worse because they have to supply graphics card CPUs and console chips.  And they are getting their raw materials from tsmc who is already tapped out....

​ @EIsenah  The 3090 is actually the 3080 performance wise, just like the 2080Ti is actually the RTX-2080 performance wise. The real 3080Ti would be about 25 to 30% faster than the 3090.

The "80Ti" tier series of cards has always been the enthusiast's absolute top end tier and has always been about 25% faster than the standard '80 class and a little more expensive than the $500 '80 class at $700. This is different from other cards like the 1070Ti or the 3060Ti. The 80Ti has always been logically the '90 Tier card at a full 25% to 30% faster that the '80 class (the standard performance jumps between tiers in the same generation; (eg GTX-1060 to GTX-1070 to GTX-1080 to 1080Ti).

Nvidia has effectively downgraded total performance by two tiers (The '80 and '80Ti classes, the Titan has always been more like a '80Ti Super with more VRAM ) and increased the prices by 3 tiers. If you do the back checking on historical generational performance jumps, you would be shocked to find that the current 3080's performance is logically where the "real 3070" should be if it were maintaining the traditional 40-50% performance gains each generation. Yet the 3080's MSRP is $650 - $700 which is traditionally '80Ti prices. So Nvidia is selling us RTX-3070 performance for what should be 3080Ti prices, with the "real 3080" (3090) sold at Titan class prices.

Of course, Nvidia couldn't have imagined in the wildest dreams that COVID would send the prices of all GPUs skyrocketing. So they are making even more money than ever. But far worse is AMD which is now on par with them, but will NEVER reduce their prices back to traditional. They want all that sweet cash too. The RX-6900XT should be the RTX-3080 equivalent at $700, but, like Nvidia, they are happy to sell them for $2000 instead..

Short story, the GPU markets are rigged against us with only two competitors and both of them have ZERO interest in returning to normal (2016) pricing. The PC gaming market is screwed as it prices itself into oblivion.

comments.text:
​ @KG993-p8m  Even AMD sponsored titles favour Nvidia in ray tracing, the gap is smaller but still present and noticeable actually, look at any benchmark that covers Godfall or RE Village. AMD gets better frames at 1440p in those titles with ray tracing turned off and then falls behind when you turn it on! That's not performing nearly the same when you lose a lead.

FSR is yet to be out in the wild, the previews shown and what we know of how the tech functions indicate it will most likely be on par with DLSS 1.0, the much maligned first implementation as it does not utilise AI or temporal data. Saying it will be built into every game is optimistic speculation since AMD have only announced 10 titles / engines that will support it this year whereas Nvidia have confirmed DLSS will be integrated into UE5. Regarding time to implement, again there is no indication that one or the other are faster, baseless speculation.

Onto VRAM, capacity is overrated, speed and bandwidth will be more important going forwards with the advent of the Direct Storage API this year and the texture streaming it will bring about. NVIDIA has a significant advantage here.
